newsitem.title: USA: Insurance agents "neutral" on US bank reform bill.
newsitem.headline: Insurance agents "neutral" on US bank reform bill.

text.p: The influential Independent Insurance Agents of America has taken a neutral stance towards bank reform legislation currently being debated by the House Banking Committee, the group's top lobbyists said on Wednesday.

The group, which represents 300,000 insurance agents, is unhappy with provisions in the bill on state regulation of bank insurance sales. In January, the agents group announced it would no longer oppose all bank reform and might support legislation that imposed "functional regulation," allowing states to regulate national banks that sold insurance.
"We're neutral on the bill," senior vice president Robert Rusbuldt told Reuters. "It's silent on functional regulation."

But if some of the provisions in the current bill are not removed or changed, the group might actively oppose the bill, top lobbyist Paul Equale told Reuters. "We would like to not have to oppose the bill," he said.
Congress has been trying to reform antiquated U.S. banking laws for over a decade, but previous efforts have collapsed when the various industry groups were unable to agree on key provisions.

That could happen again this year if the insurance agents oppose the bill, but the group will have further oportunities to make changes as the banking committee considers other amendments. If the banking panel approves the bill, the legislation then moves to the Commerce Committee for consideration.
Under a Supreme Court ruling last year, federal bank regulators can overrule state insurance rules that are seen as discriminating against banks.

A Clinton administration proposal last month would have gone even further and expanded federal preemption authority, some insurance groups said. That language was not included in the bill the banking panel is debating.

The agents group backed an amendment offered on Wednesday by Rep Rick Hill, Republican of Montana, that would have limited federal authority over state regulators. In the bill, states cannot "prevent or restrict" banks from engaging in insurance or affiliating with insurance companies.
"Many interpret that as a green light to preempt consumer laws at the state level," Rusbuldt said.
Hill's amendment would have replaced the word "restrict" with the word "preclude," thus allowing state regulators to limit but not ban bank insurance sales.
Other lawmakers objected and Hill withdrew the amendment.
The seemingly simple change would be "absolutely emasculating (to) the whole provision" allowing federal preemption, Rep Melvin Watt, Democrat of North Carolina, said.

Staffers then began work on a compromise approach that would keep the word "restrict" but would add a provision making clear that state insurance regulators could impose non-discriminatory rules on bank insurance sales.
If no compromise is reached and the word "restrict" remains, the insurance agents could turn against the bill, Equale said.
